transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I guess I’m here because I’ve been kind of stuck on something with my face. It’s probably not as bad as I make it out to be, but when I look in the mirror or see myself in photos, I keep noticing this rough, sort of sunken-looking patch—like one side of my face looks old or beat-up.

People tell me they barely notice anything, so I know maybe I’m making too much of it… but I can’t seem to stop seeing it. Does that make sense?
How much does this concern about your face bother you or interfere with your daily life, like avoiding pictures, spending a lot of time checking mirrors, or feeling anxious in social situations?

Yeah… I mean, it’s not like I’m missing work all the time or anything. But it does slow me down some mornings. I’ll get caught looking at it, trying to see if it’s as bad as I think, and then I’m late getting out the door for a construction job, which I know isn’t great.

And, uh… I’ve been kind of avoiding certain things. Like if they’re taking site photos, I try to stay out of them. And with my family, I’ve skipped a few game nights because I just didn’t want to sit there feeling like everyone was looking at my face. I know that probably sounds a little silly, but it does get to me.

When you’re looking at your face or thinking about how it looks, do you find yourself doing certain things over and over again—like checking mirrors, touching your face, comparing yourself to others, or trying to cover it up?

Yeah… I do, a little. I mean, I try not to make a big production of it, but before work or if I’m supposed to go to my sister’s game night, I’ll end up checking the bathroom mirror more than once.

I’ll kind of turn my face different ways under the light, see if that spot looks as bad as I think, and sometimes I rub at it like that’s going to help or something. And if it feels too obvious, I might wear a hat pulled down lower… or, you know, sometimes I’ll just come up with an excuse not to go. I know that probably isn’t the best way to handle it.
When you look at that part of your face, do you believe that it looks abnormal or physically deformed, even though others say they don’t notice it much?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t want to say “deformed,” because that sounds kind of extreme, and maybe I’m making it bigger than it is. But when I look at it, especially in the mirror or in pictures, it really does look wrong to me—like that rough, sunken patch makes one side of my face look old or beat-up.

And I know people tell me they barely see anything, so I’m trying to keep that in mind… but I still can’t stop seeing it that way. Does that make sense?
Have you found yourself repeatedly comparing your face to others, or spending a lot of time thinking about how your face looks — maybe even trying to analyze it or figure out how to fix it?

Yeah… I guess I do that. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there for hours or anything, but before work, or if I’m supposed to go to my sister’s game night, I’ll check the bathroom mirror a few times.

I’ll turn my face one way and then the other, try different light, like maybe it won’t look as bad from a different angle. Sometimes I catch myself rubbing at that spot too, which I know probably doesn’t do anything.

And if I feel like it’s really standing out, I might pull a hat down lower… or, honestly, just make some excuse not to go. I don’t know if that’s what you mean, but yeah, it happens.
When you’re focused on that part of your face, do you feel a strong urge to keep checking it or doing something to try to 'fix' how it looks, even if you know it might not make sense?

Yeah… I do get that urge. I try to tell myself to just leave it alone, but before work, or if I’m going to my sister’s game night, I’ll end up back at the bathroom mirror checking it again.

I’ll turn my face under the light, kind of see if it looks better or worse from another angle, and sometimes I rub at the spot even though I know that probably doesn’t fix anything. If it seems too noticeable, I’ll pull a hat down low… or, I hate to admit it, sometimes I’ll just make an excuse not to go.

I know that probably sounds a little much. I’m not trying to be difficult, it just feels hard to stop once I notice it.
Has this concern with your face ever caused you significant distress or made it hard for you to function in any part of your life, like at work, with family, or in social situations?

Yeah… I mean, I wouldn’t want to make it sound like I can’t function at all, because I do get to work and I handle my responsibilities. But it has caused problems.

There’ve been mornings where I’m late getting out the door for construction jobs because I keep checking my face or trying to make it look less noticeable. And at work I’ve started dodging site photos if someone’s taking them.

With family stuff… I’ve skipped some of my sister’s game nights, or made excuses, because I just don’t want people sitting there looking at my face. I know that probably sounds kind of silly, but it does get to me.
Has this concern about your face ever caused you to avoid social situations or activities you used to enjoy, or interfered with your relationships with others?

Yeah… a bit. I mean, I still try to show up for people, so I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

But I have skipped some of my sister’s game nights, or said I was tired or had something else going on, when really I just didn’t want everyone looking at my face. And at work, I’ve been late getting out the door sometimes because I’m trying to deal with it before I leave. I’ve also started avoiding site photos when people take them.

So… yeah, I guess it has gotten in the way some. Does that make sense?
Have you ever felt like you had to do something specific—like checking your face repeatedly, touching it, or covering it up—to feel better or to 'fix' the way it looks, even if only temporarily?

Yeah… I guess I do. I mean, I know it probably doesn’t really fix anything, but before work, or if I’m going over to my sister’s for game night, I’ll end up checking the bathroom mirror more than I should.

I’ll turn my face a little, look at it under different lights, kind of see if it’s as noticeable. Sometimes I rub at the spot, like that’s going to help, even though I know it probably won’t. And if I can’t get comfortable with it, I’ll wear a hat pulled down low… or sometimes I’ll just make an excuse not to go.

I don’t like admitting that, but yeah, it does make me feel a little better for a while.

When you think about the part of your face that bothers you, is it mainly about how it looks — like a defect or flaw in appearance — or is it more about a fear that something else might happen because of it, like health problems or others judging you in a broader way?

It’s mostly how it looks, I think. Not really that I’m scared it’s going to turn into some health thing.

It’s just… when I see it in the mirror or in photos, there’s this rough, kind of sunken-looking patch on my face, and it makes one side of me look old and beat-up. That’s what gets stuck in my head.

People tell me they barely notice anything, so I know maybe I’m making too much of it… but I still see it. Is that what you mean?
Is your concern about your face mainly focused on that specific area you described, or do you also find yourself very worried about other parts of your appearance as well?

Mostly that one area, yeah. I mean, I don’t think I’m sitting around picking apart everything about myself.

It’s really that rough, kind of sunken-looking patch on my face. In the mirror or in photos, it just jumps out at me, like one side of my face looks older or beat-up. Other people say they barely notice it, and I try to believe them… but I keep seeing it.

So, yeah, I’d say it’s mainly focused there. Does that answer it right?

When you look at that area of your face and it bothers you, do you believe that it actually looks as bad as you see it — like, in your mind, do you feel it truly is sunken or damaged, even if others don’t see it that way?

Yeah… I mean, I know people say they barely see anything, and I don’t want to sound like I’m arguing with them.

But when I look at it, especially in the mirror or in a photo, it really does look that way to me — rough and kind of sunken, like one side of my face looks older or beat-up. I guess that’s why I’m here, because I can’t seem to stop seeing it like that, even if other people don’t. Does that make sense?
